newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile remains cautious over NAFTA entry.
newsitem.headline: Chile remains cautious over NAFTA entry.

text.p: After seeing its hopes of joining NAFTA dashed last year, the Chilean government reacted cautiously on Thursday to statements by U.S. congressmen supporting Chile's entry to the giant trade bloc.

Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich supported Wednesday the extension of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) to include Chile, while Senate majority leader Trent Lott said the bloc should be extended in Latin America.
Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza made no comment on the statements Thursday and the day before had limited himself to calling Gingrich's remarks "important".

"If the news leads effectively to the passing of 'fast track,' it is obviously welcome, but we are not in any case making excessive expectations," acting Economy Minister Oscar Landerretche told influential daily El Mercurio.
Chile's hopes of becoming the fourth member of NAFTA were dashed last year after congressional discussions over "fast track" legislation died before November's presidential elections.
"Fast track" legislation allows U.S. negotiators to reach a final agreement which can either be accepted or rejected by Congress, but not modified.
Chilean officials have said they will not negotiate without "fast track" as they fear any accord would be picked apart in Congress under pressure from special interest groups.

"At this moment, (the government's) position is correct. We have already suffered once with the delay of Chile's entry to NAFTA as a result of internal North American difficulties," Alex Fernandez, president of the Chilean-North American Chamber of Commerce, told Reuters.

"The declarations are very important and we can expect a positive vote for fast track. One could expect the fast track vote within the next 90 days, but we don't know how long talks on entry to NAFTA will take," said Fernandez.
Chile's government has lowered the profile of the country's NAFTA aims, preferring to concentrate on President Eduardo Frei's forthcoming visit to the United States.
Frei, who will be in the U.S. from February 24-28, will hold talks with President Bill Clinton and address a session of Congress.
